question: What is Redis, where does it keep its data, and what kinds of application problems is it meant to solve?
model_answer: Redis is a server (a TCP daemon) that exposes abstract data types such as strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets under binary-safe keys, and is positioned as a cache, data structure server and document/vector query engine. The data set lives primarily in the computer's memory, which is what gives it low and predictable latency; disk is used only optionally for persistence. Typical uses named by the project are caching, session storage, queues and message brokering (lists, streams, pub/sub), leaderboards and counters, and real-time analytics.
required_facts: Redis is a network server that manipulates abstract data types (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, ...) stored under keys
The data set is held primarily in memory, which is the source of its speed and predictable performance
Main use cases include caching, session storage, messaging/queues and real-time analytics

answers.A: Redis is an in-memory data structure server written in C, shipped as one server binary. It keeps typed values in RAM under string keys, executes commands against them on a single main thread, and can optionally persist and replicate the result. Which application problems it is meant to solve: not stated.
answers.B: Redis is a server program (a TCP daemon) that keeps a key space of abstract data types and lets applications read and change it by sending commands over a network connection. The data set is held primarily in the computer's memory; writes can optionally also be copied to files on disk and to other Redis servers called replicas. It is aimed at developers building real-time data-driven applications, with stated uses of caching, session management, querying/sorting/analytics, messaging and interservice communication, and vector operations. Its data types serve uses such as counters, stacks and queues, leaderboards, rate limiters and event logs.
answers.C: Redis is an in-memory key-value store and data structure server: a network server that maps binary-safe string keys to typed values such as strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets. It keeps the dataset primarily in RAM; writing it to disk through RDB snapshots or the append only file is optional. It targets real-time applications where a disk database is too slow for the request path, answering reads and writes often in under a millisecond. Named uses are caching (with eviction and key expiration), session storage, queues and messaging (job queues on lists, priority queues on sorted sets, pub/sub, streams), and secondary indexing, full-text search and vector similarity search.
answers.D: Redis is a cache, data structure server, and document and vector query engine for real-time data-driven applications. It keeps its data primarily in memory, which gives very low (often sub-millisecond) latency for reads and writes, and it can optionally persist to disk. It targets caching, distributed session storage, queues and message brokering (lists, streams, pub/sub), leaderboards, counters and rate limiters, NoSQL key-value/document/time-series storage, search and query, vector storage for AI workloads, and real-time analytics.

question: Redis has two ways of persisting data to disk. What is each one for, how do they differ in durability, and which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled?
model_answer: Snapshotting (RDB) periodically dumps the whole dataset to disk when configured save points are met (a number of seconds elapsed together with a number of writes), so a crash can lose the minutes of writes since the last snapshot. The append-only file (AOF) logs the write operations applied to the dataset and gives much better durability: with the default once-per-second fsync at most about one second of writes is lost on power failure. Both can be enabled together, and if AOF is enabled at startup Redis loads the AOF because it has the better durability guarantees.
required_facts: RDB snapshotting saves the whole dataset when a save point (elapsed seconds plus number of changes) is reached, and can lose minutes of writes
AOF is an append-only log of writes with better durability (about one second of loss with the default fsync policy)
Both can be enabled at once; at startup the AOF is loaded in preference to the RDB file

answers.A: RDB is a point-in-time snapshot of the dataset written by a forked child process. AOF is a log of write commands, kept as a set of files described by a manifest: one BASE snapshot, one or more INCR files, and HISTORY files awaiting deletion. How the two differ in durability: not stated. Which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled: not stated; the only related fact is that a preload-file option loads a backup, plain RDB or AOF at startup in place of the normal data files.
answers.B: The RDB snapshot dumps the whole data set to a file, written by a forked background child when a save point (seconds elapsed and number of changes) is met or BGSAVE is issued. The Append Only File is an alternative mode that logs each write command. With snapshots alone a process failure or power outage may lose a few minutes of writes, depending on the save points; with the AOF at its default fsync policy (every second) about one second of writes can be lost on a power outage, or a single write if only the Redis process fails. Both can be on at once and each can be off. At startup the AOF is loaded when it is enabled, otherwise the snapshot is loaded; a preload-file setting overrides both.
answers.C: An RDB snapshot is a point-in-time dump of the whole dataset, written by a forked child when configured save points (enough changes and seconds) are reached; a process problem or power outage can lose a few minutes of writes, depending on the save points. The append only file is a log of every write command, replayed at startup to rebuild the dataset, and gives better durability; how often it is synced is set by appendfsync, and with everysec roughly one second of writes can be lost. When both are enabled, the append only file is loaded at startup because it has the better durability guarantees.
answers.D: Snapshotting (RDB) dumps the whole dataset to a file (dump.rdb) asynchronously when configured save points are reached (N seconds and M changes); a crash or power loss can lose the last few minutes of writes. The append-only file (AOF) logs every write command and gives much better durability: with the default everysec fsync policy at most about one second of writes is lost on power failure, or a single write if only the Redis process fails. Both can be enabled together. If AOF is enabled at startup, the AOF is the one loaded, because it has the better durability guarantees; the RDB file is loaded only when AOF is off.

question: What is the background I/O service for, what kinds of work does it take off the main thread, and what ordering guarantee does it give?
model_answer: The background I/O service exists so that operations that could block the server are performed on side threads instead of the main thread. It handles three kinds of work: closing files (where the close may actually unlink a file and be slow), fsync of the append-only file, and lazy freeing of memory. Each job type is assigned to one specific worker thread with its own queue, and a worker processes its jobs sequentially in the order they were inserted.
required_facts: It moves slow, potentially blocking operations off the main thread onto background worker threads
The job kinds are background file close, AOF fsync, and lazy freeing of memory
Each job type is bound to one worker, and jobs on a worker are processed in FIFO order

answers.A: The background I/O service is a set of worker threads in src/bio.c that take slow work off the main thread, which must never block. The work it takes is closing files, AOF fsync and lazy freeing of memory. What ordering guarantee it gives: not stated.
answers.B: The background job service in src/bio.c uses worker threads to take work off the main thread. The work it does is background close(2) calls, AOF fsync, and lazy freeing of memory. What ordering guarantee it gives is not stated.
answers.C: Not stated. A background I/O service, the work it takes off the main thread, and any ordering guarantee are not described. The only related facts given are that optional I/O threads read, parse and write sockets, and that background saves run in a forked child.
answers.D: The background I/O service runs operations that would block the server if done on the main thread. It handles three kinds of work: deferred close(2) of files (closing the last reference can mean a slow unlink), AOF fsync, and lazy freeing of memory. Each job type is assigned to one specific worker thread with its own queue (close-file, AOF, lazy-free), and a worker may handle several job types. Jobs handled by the same worker are processed strictly in insertion order, oldest first (FIFO); a creator that wants to know when its jobs finished submits a completion-request job whose response is handed back to the main thread through a pipe.

question: What is the modules system for, how is a module brought into a running server, and how does a module's own data type get saved and restored given that the core does not understand it?
model_answer: Modules let Redis be extended beyond its built-in data structures: a module is a shared library that implements new commands (and possibly new data types). It is loaded at startup with a loadmodule directive naming the library and optional arguments, and the server aborts if a module cannot be loaded; the module's load entry point initialises the API and registers each command with flags and key positions. A module-owned value is stored as a special object type whose value is managed only by the module, with a table of function pointers for serialising, deserialising, AOF-rewriting and freeing it, and in the RDB file it is tagged with a 64-bit module type ID so loading is dispatched to the right module.
required_facts: Modules extend Redis with new commands and data types beyond the built-in ones
They are loaded via loadmodule directives at startup (the server aborts if loading fails), and the module's load function registers its commands
Module values are a special object type handled through module-supplied callbacks (serialise, deserialise, AOF rewrite, free)
In RDB a module value carries a 64-bit module type ID used to dispatch loading to the owning module

answers.A: Modules extend the server through a public API declared in src/redismodule.h, which modules compile against; JSON, Search, Time Series and the probabilistic types are delivered this way from separate repositories, and vector sets is an in-tree module. Modules are loaded during startup, after cluster initialisation and before listeners open, via loadmodule lines in the configuration (the full configuration file with those lines is generated, not hand-edited). Whether a module can be loaded into an already running server by command: not stated. A module value's encoding is owned by the module, and modules can use key metadata slots 1 to 7; how a module's data type is saved and restored: not stated.
answers.B: Modules extend Redis beyond its built-in data structures and let new commands be implemented quickly; a module is a shared library loaded into redis-server at runtime. It is named with a loadmodule line in the configuration, which is queued by queueLoadModule at startup and then loaded when main calls moduleLoadFromQueue (outside Sentinel mode). External modules are pinned in modules/modules.yaml, fetched with make modules-update and built by make, while vector sets are an in-tree module. How a module registers its commands, and how a module's own data type is saved and restored, is not stated.
answers.C: The modules API lets developers add new commands and data types beyond the built-in ones. A module is a shared library loaded into redis-server, for example with a loadmodule line in the configuration, so it is loaded at startup; loading into an already running server by command is not stated. How a module's own data type is saved and restored is not stated.
answers.D: Modules extend Redis beyond the built-in data structures: a shared library can register new commands and new native data types through the modules API. A module is loaded at startup with one or more loadmodule directives (path plus optional arguments), and the server aborts if it cannot load one; the library's RedisModule_OnLoad entry point then registers its commands and types. A module command for managing modules at runtime exists but is blocked by default by enable-module-command (no/yes/local); its exact syntax is not stated. For a module data type the core stores the value as an opaque OBJ_MODULE object: when saving it writes the module type id as a prefix, calls the type's rdb_save callback, and appends an EOF marker; when loading it reads the id, looks up the registered type, and calls its rdb_load callback, reporting an error if no matching module type is loaded. For AOF rewrite the type's optional aof_rewrite callback emits commands that rebuild the value.

question: How do the event loop, the connection layer and the client-handling code fit together to make the server run? Describe what one turn of the main loop does.
model_answer: The server is driven by a single event loop that multiplexes file (socket) events and time events over the best polling facility the OS offers (evport, epoll, kqueue, or select as fallback). At initialisation the server registers a periodic timer callback (the server cron), a before-sleep hook, and accept handlers on its listeners; each accepted client gets a read handler installed on its connection, and connections are an abstraction with pluggable types (TCP, Unix socket, TLS). Each turn of the loop runs the before-sleep hook, blocks in the poll call until a descriptor is ready or the next timer is due, runs the after-sleep hook, dispatches the fired read/write handlers, and finally runs due time events.
required_facts: A single event loop handles both file (socket) events and time events, choosing one OS polling backend (evport/epoll/kqueue/select) at build time
Server init registers the periodic cron timer, a before-sleep hook and accept handlers; each client connection gets a read handler
One iteration: before-sleep hook, poll (sleeping until an fd fires or the next timer), after-sleep hook, fired file handlers, then time events
Connections are abstracted behind a connection-type interface (TCP, Unix, TLS)

answers.A: The main thread runs one event loop from src/ae.c, with one OS backend compiled in (epoll, kqueue, evport or select). Before each poll, beforeSleep() handles pending TLS and decompressed data, cluster and slot-migration housekeeping, blocked clients, a fast expire cycle, the AOF flush, pending client writes, hand-off to I/O threads and asynchronous client frees, then releases the modules GIL. After the poll, afterSleep() reacquires the GIL first; when a connection is readable, readQueryFromClient() in src/networking.c reads into the client's query buffer, the input is parsed into commands, executed, and replies go to the client's output buffer to be written from beforeSleep() or by an I/O thread. A timer, serverCron(), runs at a rate set by hz for client timeouts, database maintenance (expiry, rehashing, defrag), replication cron and persistence triggers. Connection types are initialised at startup, but how the connection layer itself is structured: not stated.
answers.B: The event loop in src/ae.c is aeMain, which repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents; each turn runs beforeSleep, waits in aeApiPoll for ready sockets, runs afterSleep, then runs the file (socket) events and time events. On the connection side, connSocketAcceptHandler accepts a socket and hands it to acceptCommonHandler, which rejects it at maxclients or calls createClient, which installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler. When a socket is readable the loop calls that handler, which reads into the query buffer, parses it in processInputBuffer and dispatches to processCommand. The time event runs serverCron (server.hz times per second) for active expiry, rehashing, starting saves and replication reconnection. beforeSleep flushes the AOF and then sends buffered replies through handleClientsWithPendingWrites and writeToClient; a ready socket normally fires its read handler before its write handler, and AE_BARRIER inverts that. How the connection layer abstracts different transports is not stated.
answers.C: The event loop, built on the library in ae.c, sleeps until file descriptors are ready and then processes their events; aeMain repeats this until the loop is stopped. The listening socket's handler connSocketAcceptHandler accepts a TCP connection and passes it to acceptCommonHandler, which creates a client; createClient installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler, so the loop calls it when bytes arrive. That handler fills the query buffer and processInputBuffer parses and dispatches commands, whose replies go into the client output buffer. Before the loop waits again, beforeSleep flushes the append only file buffer to disk and then calls handleClientsWithPendingWrites to send buffered replies. serverCron periodically checks save points. A fuller per-turn ordering (timers, other before/after-sleep work) is not stated.
answers.D: The event loop (ae) multiplexes file-descriptor events and timers; the connection layer wraps each socket in a connection object whose type (TCP, Unix, TLS) supplies read/write/accept handlers registered with the event loop; the client code reads queries from connections, parses them, runs commands and queues replies. One turn of the loop first calls beforeSleep, which processes pending TLS data, runs cluster housekeeping, handles unblocked clients, runs a fast expire cycle on masters, flushes the AOF buffer to disk, writes pending replies to clients (or hands them to I/O threads), frees clients queued for closing, and releases the module GIL. It then polls the OS for ready descriptors, sleeping at most until the next timer is due, and on wake-up calls afterSleep (reacquire the module GIL, refresh cached time). It then fires the handlers for each ready descriptor, normally readable before writable (inverted when the barrier flag is set), and finally runs due time events such as the periodic server cron.

question: How is a database's keyspace organised in memory: what containers hold keys and their expirations, how does that layout change in cluster mode, and where is a key's name stored relative to its value?
model_answer: Each database holds a main keyspace store, a second store indexing the keys that have a timeout, and a third structure for sub-key expirations (currently hash fields), plus bookkeeping tables for blocked and watched keys. The stores are 'kvstores': an array of hash tables rather than a single one. In standalone mode there is one hash table; in cluster mode there is one per hash slot (2^14 of them, allocated on demand), so all keys of a slot can be reached easily. The key name is not a separate object: the key (and optional metadata such as the expiry, and small string values) is embedded in the same allocation as the value object.
required_facts: A database has a main keys store plus a separate store for keys with an expiration (and one for sub-key/hash-field expirations)
Each store is an array of hash tables: one table in standalone mode, one per hash slot in cluster mode
The key string (and optional expiry metadata) is embedded in the same allocation as the value object

answers.A: Each database holds two kvstore instances, keys and expires; a kvstore is an array of dicts. In cluster mode there is one dict per hash slot (16,384); otherwise there is one dict. A Fenwick tree over the dict sizes makes finding the Nth key and the next non-empty slot cheap. A third structure, subexpires, tracks hashes that have fields with a TTL, keyed by their earliest field expiry. The key name is embedded directly after the stored object's struct (a small string value may be embedded too), and the key's expiry time sits in metadata slot 0 placed before the struct.
answers.B: Not stated. The only supported facts are that keys are binary-safe strings naming values, and that a value is an object holding its type, encoding, LRU or LFU data, a refcount and a pointer to the payload; the containers for keys and expirations, the cluster-mode layout and where the key name sits relative to the value are not stated.
answers.C: Not stated beyond the basics: a server holds a keyspace in memory in which each key is a binary-safe string naming one value, and in cluster mode keys are divided over 16384 hash slots by the CRC16 of the key. The containers that hold keys and expirations, how that layout changes in cluster mode, and where the key name is stored relative to its value are not stated.
answers.D: Each database has a 'keys' kvstore holding all keys and an 'expires' kvstore holding the keys that have a timeout, plus a 'subexpires' store for sub-key (hash field) timeouts. A kvstore is an array of hash tables (dicts): in standalone mode it has a single dict, while in cluster mode it has one dict per hash slot (16384), allocated on demand and freed when empty. The dict entries are kvobj objects, which unify key and value: the key name is embedded inline in the same allocation right after the object header, and a small string value can be embedded after the key. The expiry time, when present, is stored as an 8-byte metadata field placed just before the object header, and the expires kvstore refers to the same kvobj.

question: A stored value has both a 'type' and an 'encoding'. What is the difference, why do both exist, and who decides which encoding a value uses?
model_answer: The type is the logical data type the user sees (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, stream, module value, ...), while the encoding says which in-memory representation currently implements it. Several types have multiple encodings optimised for memory footprint or speed: for example compact listpack or integer-set forms for small collections versus hash tables and skiplists for large ones, and integer or embedded forms for short strings. The generic object code only chooses encodings for strings; for the other types, the code implementing each type's commands picks and converts the encoding as the value grows. A sorted set in its full form, for instance, keeps the same elements in both a hash table (element to score) and a skiplist (ordered by score).
required_facts: Type is the logical data type; encoding is the current in-memory representation of that value
One type can have several encodings, trading memory footprint against speed (compact forms for small values, hash table/skiplist forms for large)
String encodings are chosen in the generic object code; other types' encodings are managed by the code implementing that type's commands

answers.A: A value object carries a type, an encoding, a reference count and a pointer. The type is the kind of value (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, stream, array, module); the encoding is the in-memory representation used for it, for example listpack or hash table for a set. Both exist because a type usually has a compact encoding for small values and a general one for larger ones. The switch is governed by thresholds set in redis.conf; for module types the encoding is owned by the module. Beyond those thresholds, who decides the encoding of a given value: not stated.
answers.B: The type is what a value is: an abstract data type such as a string, list, set or hash, defined by its operations and their complexity. The encoding is how that value is represented in memory at the moment, recorded in the object's encoding field; strings may be RAW, EMBSTR or INT, sets may be INTSET or HT, lists use a quicklist (a linked list of listpacks) and streams a radix tree of listpacks. Both exist so that small values can use memory-saving compact representations under the same type. A value stays in its compact form until it passes configured limits such as hash-max-listpack-entries, hash-max-listpack-value, set-max-intset-entries, set-max-listpack-entries and zset-max-listpack-entries. Which piece of code makes the choice is not stated.
answers.C: Not stated. A data type is described only as the kind of value a key holds (string, list, set, hash, sorted set); encodings, why both exist, and who chooses the encoding are not described.
answers.D: The type is the logical data type the user sees (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, stream, module, ...) and determines which commands apply. The encoding is an implementation detail: which in-memory representation currently backs that value (for example raw/embstr/int for strings, intset/listpack/hash table for sets, listpack/skiplist for sorted sets, quicklist for lists). Both exist because several types have multiple representations optimised for memory footprint or speed, so a small value can use a compact form and switch to a general one as it grows. The encoding is chosen and converted by the server's own type implementation code, driven by configured size thresholds, not by the client.

question: How is the clustering code divided, and how does a cluster node decide which hash slot a key belongs to and whether it should serve the command or redirect the client?
model_answer: The clustering code is split into a common part shared by any clustering implementation (key-space handling, slot computation, deciding which node serves a query) and a separate part implementing the standard cluster-bus based mechanism. A key maps to one of 16384 slots by taking the low 14 bits of the CRC16 of the key; if the key contains a non-empty {...} section only that part is hashed, so related keys can be forced into the same slot. For each command with keys the node works out the owning node: if it is itself the command runs, otherwise the client gets a MOVED or ASK redirection, and commands whose keys fall in different slots are refused.
required_facts: Cluster code is split into a generic/common part and a part specific to the cluster-bus (gossip) implementation
There are 16384 slots; slot = CRC16(key) reduced to 14 bits
If the key contains a non-empty {...} hash tag only the tagged part is hashed
Commands for slots owned elsewhere are redirected (MOVED/ASK); keys spanning different slots are rejected

answers.A: src/cluster.c holds the parts common to any clustering implementation: slot calculation, redirection decisions and generic CLUSTER subcommands. src/cluster_legacy.c is the standard gossip-based cluster bus: node table, failure detection, failover and config epochs; atomic slot migration and per-slot statistics are separate files. A key's slot is the CRC16 of the key, or of the text inside {...} if present, masked to 14 bits. The redirection check runs in the command gate after command lookup, arity, authentication and ACL checks, and is driven partly by the command's key specs. The rule by which a node decides to serve or redirect: not stated.
answers.B: Cluster code lives in src/cluster.c and src/cluster_legacy.c (with slot migration in src/cluster_asm.c); cluster.c covers routing and redirection, and the code as a whole maps keys to slots, routes requests and handles node failure, but exactly which responsibilities sit in which file is not stated. keyHashSlot takes the crc16 of the key and keeps its low 14 bits, giving one of 16384 slots; if the key has a {...} part only that part is hashed, so related keys can share a slot. processCommand calls getNodeByQuery, which returns the node serving that slot: if it is this node the command runs here, otherwise clusterRedirectClient replies with a MOVED error, or ASK during a migration, giving the slot and the node's address. Keys in different slots get -CROSSSLOT and a multi-key request during a slot migration can get -TRYAGAIN.
answers.C: A key belongs to one of 16384 hash slots, given by the CRC16 of the key name; the mapping is defined in src/cluster.h. During command checking, processCommand redirects the client when the key is owned by another cluster node, and otherwise the command proceeds; multi-key operations work only when all keys share a slot. Cluster nodes talk to each other on a separate bus port. How the clustering code is divided into files or layers is not stated.
answers.D: cluster.c holds the parts common to any clustering implementation (key-to-slot handling, routing a query to a node, redirections), while cluster_legacy.c implements the standard cluster-bus (gossip) based mechanism; slot statistics and atomic slot migration have their own units. A key's slot is CRC16 of the key masked to 14 bits (16384 slots); if the key contains a non-empty {...} section, only the text between the first '{' and the next '}' is hashed. For a command, the node checks that all keys map to one slot (otherwise a cross-slot error), finds the node owning that slot, and serves it if that is itself; otherwise it replies with a MOVED redirection. If the slot is migrating and some keys are missing it replies ASK (or TRYAGAIN for multi-key requests with only some keys present); an importing node serves only clients that sent ASKING; an unbound slot or a down cluster gives a cluster-down error; a read-only client on a replica can be served for its master's slots.

question: Walk through what happens to a write command from the moment its bytes arrive on a client socket until it has been executed and made durable or replicated. What checks can stop it before execution?
model_answer: The connection's read handler reads bytes into the client's query buffer and the input-buffer processor parses complete commands into an argument vector. The command processor then looks the command up in the command table and rejects unknown names or wrong arity, checks authentication and ACL permissions, performs cluster redirection if the keys belong to another node, tries to evict data if memory is over the limit (rejecting with an out-of-memory error if it cannot), and refuses writes when persistence is failing, when too few replicas are connected, or when the node is a read-only replica. If the client is inside a transaction the command is queued instead; otherwise the core call routine executes it and, if it changed the dataset, propagates it to the AOF buffer and to the replication stream. The AOF buffer is written to disk in the before-sleep hook, before replies are delivered to clients.
required_facts: Bytes are read into a per-client query buffer and parsed into arguments before the command is looked up in the command table (unknown command / wrong arity rejected)
Pre-execution checks include authentication/ACL, cluster redirection, maxmemory eviction (OOM rejection), and write refusals (disk error, not enough replicas, read-only replica)
Inside MULTI the command is queued instead of executed
After execution a data-modifying command is propagated to the AOF buffer and to replicas; the AOF buffer is flushed before returning to the event loop / replying

answers.A: When the connection becomes readable, readQueryFromClient() reads the bytes into the client's query buffer, and processInputBuffer() parses RESP or inline input into pending command objects, parsing ahead so key lookups for pipelined commands can be prefetched. processCommand() then applies checks in a fixed order, any of which can stop the command: command lookup and arity, authentication, ACL, cluster redirection, client-memory eviction, maxmemory eviction, disk-error and min-replicas write refusal, read-only replica, pub/sub context, stale replica, loading, busy script and client pause; inside MULTI the command is queued instead of executed. call() runs the handler, records stats and slowlog, and propagates the write to the AOF and to replicas. The AOF is flushed before the event loop's next poll, with fsync done by a background thread, and the reply is written from the same pre-poll step or by an I/O thread.
answers.B: The event loop calls readQueryFromClient when the socket is readable; it reads bytes into the query buffer and processInputBuffer parses them (input starting with * as multibulk, otherwise inline) into a pending command; an I/O thread may read and parse but must queue the client for the main thread. processCommand looks the command up and can refuse it for: authentication required, ACL denial (-NOPERM), cluster routing to another node (redirect), failed eviction for a deny-on-memory-limit command (OOM error), a disk persistence error, a write on a read-only replica, or the server still loading data. Otherwise call runs the command's handler (setCommand for SET, which stores the key, raises server.dirty and queues the OK reply). Because dirty changed, the command is queued with alsoPropagate and sent to both feedAppendOnlyFile (into the AOF buffer) and replicationFeedSlaves when the outermost unit finishes, with several commands from one unit wrapped in MULTI/EXEC. Just before the loop sleeps, beforeSleep flushes the AOF buffer to the file first, then sends the buffered reply to the client.
answers.C: The event loop calls readQueryFromClient, which fills the client's query buffer and calls processInputBuffer; that chooses between the multibulk protocol (input starting with *) and inline commands, parses arguments, and calls processCommandAndResetClient once a full command is ready. processCommand looks up the command, checks ACL permissions, redirects keys owned by another cluster node, runs eviction when maxmemory is set, and refuses writes after a persistence error; with no evictable key under the memory limit, writes needing memory get errors. Inside MULTI the command is queued and answered QUEUED; otherwise call runs the command's proc function, which writes its reply with addReply into the output buffer. After a write, call hands the command to alsoPropagate, and propagateNow feeds it to feedAppendOnlyFile (a memory buffer) and replicationFeedSlaves (the replication stream). In beforeSleep, flushAppendOnlyFile writes the buffer to disk before handleClientsWithPendingWrites sends the replies; fsync frequency follows appendfsync.
answers.D: The connection's read handler reads bytes into the client's query buffer, the buffer is parsed (multibulk or inline protocol) into an argument vector, and the command is looked up in the command table. question: How does a background rewrite of the append-only file work, step by step, and how does the server keep track of which files make up the log while writes continue?
model_answer: The append-only log is a set of files tracked by a manifest: at most one base file (a snapshot as of the last rewrite), one or more incremental files holding the writes since then, and history files left over from earlier generations. On a rewrite the parent first flushes its buffer and opens a new incremental file to keep logging, then forks; the child writes a fresh snapshot of the dataset to a temporary file and exits. When the parent sees the child succeeded, it renames the temporary file to a new base file name, marks the previous base and the already-covered incremental files as history, persists the updated manifest, and deletes the history files in a background thread.

History files are deleted afterwards in the background

question: When a replica connects (or reconnects) to a master, how does the master decide between sending only the missing data and doing a full resynchronization, and what happens in each case?
model_answer: The replica asks to continue from a given replication ID and offset. The master accepts a partial resynchronization only if that ID matches its current replication ID (or its secondary ID, up to the offset where that history ended) and the requested offset is still inside its replication backlog, an in-memory buffer of recent replication stream; it then replies that it can continue and sends the backlog from that offset onward. Otherwise it falls back to a full resynchronization: it tells the replica the new replication ID and offset, produces an RDB snapshot in a forked child (written to disk and then transferred, or streamed directly to replica sockets in diskless mode), and the replica loads it. A bigger backlog lets replicas survive longer disconnections without a full resync.

Partial resync also requires the requested offset to still be covered by the replication backlog buffer; then only the missing backlog portion is sent
Otherwise a full resync happens: the master announces a new ID/offset and transfers an RDB snapshot produced by a child process (via disk or directly over the socket)

In a full sync using the RDB channel, the replica opens a second connection so the forked child streams the RDB directly while the main connection carries live writes, which the replica buffers until loading finishes; this moves buffering pressure from primary to replica. What happens step by step in the partial case beyond using the backlog: not stated.

On the master, syncCommand calls masterTryPartialResynchronization, which accepts when the replication ID matches and the requested offset is still inside the replication backlog; it then answers +CONTINUE and the replica gets only the part it missed. Otherwise the master answers +FULLRESYNC, runs startBgsaveForReplication to produce an RDB, and the replica receives that RDB in readSyncBulkPayload. In both cases the master afterwards streams write commands through replicationFeedSlaves, and a replica passes its master's stream unchanged to its own replicas.

The master keeps a replication backlog, a buffer of recent writes; after a short disconnect the replica can resume from that backlog with a partial resync and receive only what it missed, instead of copying everything again. Otherwise a full resynchronization is done. The exact conditions the master tests (such as IDs or offsets) and the steps of a full resynchronization are not stated.

The master accepts a partial resync only if that ID matches its current replication ID (or its second, previous ID with the offset not beyond the point where that ID stopped being valid) and the requested offset still lies inside the replication backlog. In that case it marks the client as an online replica, replies +CONTINUE, and sends the backlog bytes from that offset onward. Otherwise (ID mismatch, offset outside the backlog, no backlog, or the replica asked with '?') it does a full resync: it replies +FULLRESYNC with its ID and offset, produces an RDB snapshot via a background save (to disk then transferred, or diskless straight to the socket, possibly reusing an in-progress save or waiting for the next one), and then streams the writes buffered since the snapshot. question: How do keys with a time-to-live actually get removed? Describe the mechanisms involved, how the background one limits its own cost, and how removal is kept consistent on replicas and in the append-only file.
model_answer: Expired keys are reclaimed in two ways: lazily, when a key is accessed and found to be past its expiry, and actively, by a background cycle that samples keys with timeouts so that keys never accessed again are still freed. The active cycle is adaptive and runs in two forms: a slow cycle from the periodic server timer (hz times per second) bounded to a percentage of CPU time, and a short fast cycle run before each sleep of the event loop, bounded to about a millisecond; it stops working on a database once the estimated fraction of expired keys is low. Only the master deletes: when it removes an expired key it sends an explicit delete to replicas and the AOF, while replicas do not delete expired keys themselves but report them as expired to readers until the master's delete arrives.

The active cycle has a slow form run from the periodic timer and a fast form run before sleeping, each with a time limit, and is adaptive to how many keys are expired
The master propagates a delete (DEL/UNLINK) for each expired key to replicas and the AOF
Replicas do not delete expired keys on their own; they wait for the master's delete while still treating the key as logically expired for reads

How removal is kept consistent on replicas and in the append-only file: not stated specifically; the general rule is that any write must be propagated exactly as it should replay.

question: Why does eviction pick victims using an approximation instead of tracking exact least-recently-used order, how does the approximation work, and what does that choice cost?
model_answer: Exact LRU ordering would need extra memory per key, so Redis uses an approximation that runs in constant memory: each object carries only a small access clock (or frequency counter), and when a key must be evicted the server samples a handful of keys (five by default) and feeds the best candidates into a small fixed-size pool kept across eviction calls, then evicts the best entry in the pool. The cost is accuracy: the evicted key is not guaranteed to be the globally oldest one. The sample size is tunable to trade CPU for accuracy (ten samples comes very close to true LRU but costs more CPU, three is faster but less accurate).

It samples a small number of keys (default 5) and keeps the best candidates in a small fixed-size pool across calls, evicting the best one
The trade-off is accuracy versus CPU, tunable via the sample size (more samples = closer to true LRU but more CPU)

Each value object carries LRU or LFU data used for the choice. The cost is that victim selection is not exact, with accuracy traded against CPU; the internal working of the sampling is not stated.

Why an approximation was chosen over exact ordering, how the approximation works in detail, and what it costs are not stated.

The cost is accuracy: the victim is not guaranteed to be the true least-recently-used key. A sample size of 10 approximates true LRU very closely but uses more CPU, 3 is faster but not very accurate, and the maximum is 64.

question: Why are the main hash tables resized incrementally rather than all at once, and why is resizing discouraged while a background save or rewrite child is running? What does each choice cost?
model_answer: Rehashing is spread over many small steps (one bucket at a time, piggybacked on ordinary lookups and updates, plus about one millisecond of active rehashing ten times a second) so that growing a huge table never blocks the single main thread for a long time; the cost is that two tables coexist and use extra memory until rehashing finishes, and active rehashing can add occasional small delays. While a forked child is saving, resizing is avoided because the child shares memory pages with the parent copy-on-write, and moving lots of entries would cause many pages to be copied. The cost of that is that tables may run denser than ideal during a save; resizing is only forced when the load factor exceeds a hard ratio, and inside the child itself it is forbidden entirely.

The cost of incremental rehashing is extra memory while two tables coexist (and small latency from active rehashing)
With a child process active, resizing is avoided to limit copy-on-write page copying
Resizing is still allowed when the fill ratio passes a forced threshold (elements/buckets of 4 or more)

answers.A: The main thread must never block, so long work is done incrementally; rehashing is carried out in the periodic database maintenance step. Why resizing is discouraged while a background save or rewrite child runs: not stated. What each choice costs: not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. The only supported fact is that rehashing is one of the periodic jobs serverCron performs; the reasons for incremental resizing, the interaction with a background save or rewrite child, and the costs are not stated.
answers.C: Not stated. Hash table resizing, incremental rehashing, and its interaction with a background save or rewrite child are not described.
answers.D: Rehashing a large table in one step would block the server for a long time, so buckets are moved a few at a time: one step on each lookup or update of a table that is rehashing, plus an active rehash that spends about 1 millisecond in every 100 milliseconds of CPU time. The cost is that two tables coexist during rehash, using more memory, that an idle server never finishes rehashing without active rehashing, and that active rehashing can add delays of up to about 2 milliseconds to replies. The cost of that is fuller tables: growth is then allowed only once the elements-to-buckets ratio reaches 4, and shrinking only when the table is extremely sparse (1/32); inside the child itself resizing is forbidden.

question: Why does Redis execute commands on essentially one thread, where does it nevertheless use extra threads, and what are the stated costs or conditions of doing so?
model_answer: The project's stated philosophy is that threading is not a silver bullet: an efficient, mostly single-threaded core is simpler, and scaling is achieved by running several such shared-nothing instances combined by higher-level features like Redis Cluster, which also keeps each instance's dataset small enough for persist-by-fork to work well. Parallelism was only considered worthwhile for I/O, the low-hanging fruit. Accordingly, optional I/O threads handle client socket reads, protocol parsing and writes while command execution stays on the main thread (I/O threads hand clients back to the main thread and never free clients themselves), and other side threads handle things like lazy freeing and slow file operations. I/O threading is off by default and recommended only on machines with at least four cores, leaving a spare core, and only when CPU is actually the bottleneck.
required_facts: The core is deliberately (mostly) single-threaded for simplicity; scaling comes from multiple shared-nothing instances (e.g. Redis Cluster)
Extra threads are used only for I/O (socket reads, parsing, writes) and background chores such as lazy freeing; command execution stays on the main thread
I/O threads are disabled by default and advised only with 4+ cores and a real CPU bottleneck

Replication stream compression is only effective with more than one I/O thread.

Costs and conditions: one slow operation (a huge aggregated value, a long script) blocks everything else; I/O threads do not make commands run in parallel and are recommended only when the instance really has CPU-bound performance problems; pub/sub, monitor, blocked and tracking clients stay on the main thread; and multi-threaded I/O is documented as unsupported for TLS, although a code comment suggests otherwise, so that should be checked. Helper threads are started after modules load because of a race between thread-local storage setup and dlopen.

Extra threads are used as optional I/O threads that read, parse and write sockets, and background saves use a forked child process. Extra threads are used for background jobs (closing files, AOF fsync, lazy freeing for UNLINK and async flushes), optionally for client socket reads, protocol parsing and writes (io-threads), for the allocator's background thread, and by module threads that take a global lock to touch the dataset while the main thread sleeps. Threaded I/O is disabled by default; it is suggested only on machines with at least 4 cores, leaving at least one core spare (for example 3 threads on 4 cores), and only if the instance really is CPU-bound, otherwise there is no point. Setting io-threads to 1 uses just the main thread.

question: What trade-off do the append-only file's sync policies offer, why is the log written just before the event loop sleeps rather than inside each command, and what durability is given up while a background save is running if the related mitigation is turned on?
model_answer: There are three fsync policies: never (let the OS flush when it wants: fastest, least safe), every write (slow, safest) and once per second (the default compromise). Because a client must not get a reply before its write is in the log, and replies can only go out when the event loop is re-entered, all AOF writes of an iteration are accumulated in a memory buffer and written just before sleeping; with the always policy a write barrier ensures a socket is not read and replied to in the same iteration before that flush. Since fsync can block for a long time while a child is doing heavy disk I/O, an option lets the server skip fsync during a background save or rewrite, which reduces latency but means durability is temporarily the same as the never policy (up to about 30 seconds of log could be lost with default Linux settings).
required_facts: Three policies: no fsync (fastest), always (safest, slow), every second (default compromise)
AOF writes are buffered and flushed just before re-entering the event loop so the log is written before the client is answered
Skipping fsync during a background save/rewrite trades durability (equivalent to no fsync, up to ~30 s of loss) for lower latency

answers.A: The append-only file is flushed in the step that runs before each event-loop poll, and fsync is done by a background thread. What trade-off the sync policies offer: not stated. Why the log is written before the loop sleeps rather than inside each command: not stated. What durability is given up during a background save with the mitigation turned on: not stated.
answers.B: The appendfsync policy trades speed for safety: no never fsyncs and lets the OS flush (fastest), always fsyncs after every write (slow, safest), and everysec, the default, fsyncs once per second as a compromise that can lose about one second of writes. Commands append to an in-memory AOF buffer, and the buffer is written by flushAppendOnlyFile from beforeSleep, ahead of sending replies, so that with always the write reaches the file before the reply goes out. With always, a failed write makes the process exit because the reply may already be buffered and the change cannot be rolled back. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite set to yes, up to 30 seconds of log can be lost in the worst case with default Linux settings.
answers.C: appendfsync sets how often the log is fsynced, trading durability against disk I/O; everysec fsyncs once per second as a compromise and can lose about one second of writes. The other policy values are not stated. Writes are appended to a memory buffer and flushAppendOnlyFile writes it to disk in beforeSleep, before replies are sent, because the log must be written before replying to the client. What durability is given up during a background save when the related mitigation is turned on is not stated.
answers.D: The policies trade speed for safety: 'always' fsyncs after every write to the log (slow, safest), 'everysec' fsyncs once per second (the default compromise, can lose about a second), and 'no' leaves flushing to the operating system (fastest). The log must be written before the client is answered, and a client socket can only be written from the event loop, so writes are accumulated in a memory buffer and flushed in one go just before re-entering the event loop, ahead of sending replies. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite set to yes, fsync is not called in the main process while a background save or log rewrite is running, so durability during that time equals 'appendfsync no' and up to about 30 seconds of log can be lost in the worst case with default Linux settings. The option exists because fsync can block too long while a child is doing heavy disk I/O.

question: Where is it decided when a small hash, set, sorted set or list stops using its compact representation, and how would you tune or change that behaviour?

required_facts: Thresholds are configuration directives: max entries and max entry size for the compact form of hashes, sets and sorted sets (plus an integer-set limit for sets and a per-node size for lists)
The conversion is carried out in each data type's own implementation when a write exceeds the threshold (e.g. hash converts listpack to hash table)
Default limits: hashes 512 entries / 64-byte values; sets and sorted sets 128 entries / 64 bytes

answers.A: Each type has a compact encoding for small values and a general one, and the thresholds between them are settings in redis.conf, so tuning means changing those settings. The type's own file (t_hash.c, t_set.c, t_zset.c, t_list.c) implements its encodings. For hashes, automatic conversion to the template encoding is controlled by hash-min-template-entries, which is 0 (off) by default and one-way. The exact function where the conversion decision is made, and the names of the other thresholds: not stated.
answers.B: The switch away from the compact form is governed by configuration limits: hash-max-listpack-entries and hash-max-listpack-value for hashes, set-max-intset-entries and set-max-listpack-entries for sets, and zset-max-listpack-entries for sorted sets; a value stays compact until it passes them. Tuning is done by changing those settings in the configuration. Where in the code the conversion decision is made is not stated, and no threshold for lists is stated (lists are a linked list of listpacks).
answers.C: Not stated. Compact representations of small hashes, sets, sorted sets or lists, and the thresholds for leaving them, are not described.
answers.D: The decision is made in each type's implementation file (hash, set, sorted set and list code) when elements are added, and again when values are loaded from an RDB file; these compare the element count and element size against server settings. The thresholds are hash-max-listpack-entries (512) and hash-max-listpack-value (64), set-max-intset-entries (512), set-max-listpack-entries (128) and set-max-listpack-value (64), zset-max-listpack-entries (128) and zset-max-listpack-value (64), and list-max-listpack-size (-2, meaning 8 KB per list node; positive values mean an element count). They are defined in the configuration table as runtime-modifiable, so they can be tuned in the configuration file or changed live. Changing the rule itself, rather than the numbers, means editing the conversion checks in the type files and the matching checks in the RDB loading code.

question: Where would you plug in (a) support for a different operating-system readiness-notification API and (b) a new kind of client transport alongside TCP, Unix sockets and TLS?
model_answer: The polling backend is selected at compile time inside the event-loop library: it includes exactly one backend implementation file, tried in order of expected performance (evport, epoll, kqueue, then select), so a new OS API means a new backend file plus a new branch in that selection. A transport is added by implementing the connection-type interface (a table of callbacks for init, configure, accept, read/write handlers, address lookup and so on) and registering it with the connection-type registry, which holds a small fixed number of types keyed by name. TCP and Unix types are mandatory at startup, while TLS registration may fail when the server is built without TLS support.
required_facts: The OS polling backend is a compile-time choice inside the event-loop library, one implementation file per API, ordered by performance
A transport is an implementation of the connection-type callback interface registered by name in a registry
TCP and Unix socket types are required; TLS is optional and depends on a build flag

answers.A: (a) The event library in src/ae.c compiles in one backend from ae_epoll.c, ae_kqueue.c, ae_evport.c or ae_select.c, so a new readiness API would be another backend file of that kind. (b) Connection types are initialised during startup, before the configuration is parsed; where a new transport is defined or registered: not stated.
answers.B: (a) The event loop in src/ae.c selects its multiplexing layer from separate backend files, trying ae_evport.c, then ae_epoll.c, then ae_kqueue.c, and falling back to ae_select.c, so a new readiness API would be another such backend chosen in src/ae.c. (b) The TCP accept path is connSocketAcceptHandler in src/socket.c, which hands sockets to acceptCommonHandler, and TLS can be built in or built as a module; where a new transport type is registered is not stated.
answers.C: Not stated. The event loop is built on the library in ae.c and connections are accepted by connSocketAcceptHandler and handed to acceptCommonHandler, with TLS optional via BUILD_TLS=yes, but where a new readiness-notification backend or a new transport type would be plugged in is not described.
answers.D: (a) Each readiness API is a separate backend file (evport, epoll, kqueue, select) implementing the same small set of static functions: create, resize, free, add event, delete event, poll and name. The event loop source includes exactly one of them at compile time, chosen by feature macros set in the build configuration header, in the order evport, epoll, kqueue, then select as fallback; a new API means a new backend file plus a branch in that selection and its detection macro. (b) A transport is a ConnectionType: a struct of function pointers for init/configure, listen/accept, connect, read/write/writev, handler registration, sync I/O, event-loop rebinding, pending data and peer identity. A new transport defines such a struct in its own file, provides a registration function that calls connTypeRegister, and is added to connTypeInitialize alongside the socket, Unix and TLS registrations.

question: What happens when the configured memory limit is reached, in which situations will writes start failing, and what memory or which instances are not subject to the limit in the way you might expect?
model_answer: When memory use exceeds the limit, Redis tries before executing commands to evict keys according to the selected policy, for a bounded time per call so the server stays responsive (continuing in a timer if needed). If the policy is no-eviction (the default) or no suitable key exists (for example a volatile policy with no keys that have a TTL), commands that would use more memory are rejected with an error while reads keep working. Replica output buffers and AOF buffers are deliberately not counted as used memory, to avoid a feedback loop where eviction deletes fill the buffers and trigger more eviction; so real memory can exceed the limit and headroom should be left. Replicas by default ignore the limit entirely and just follow the master's deletes, so they can use more memory than configured.
required_facts: On reaching the limit, keys are evicted per the configured policy; eviction work is time-bounded per call
With the no-eviction policy (the default) or when nothing is evictable, memory-increasing write commands get an error while reads continue
Replica output buffers and AOF buffers are excluded from the counted memory to avoid an eviction feedback loop
Replicas ignore maxmemory by default and may exceed it

answers.A: A maxmemory eviction step runs in the command gate before a command executes, preceded by a separate client-memory eviction step, and a command's denyoom flag is among the flags that drive that gate. Exactly what happens when the limit is reached, in which situations writes fail, and which memory or instances are not subject to the limit: not stated.
answers.B: When maxmemory is set, processCommand calls performEvictions before running a command, which frees keys according to maxmemory-policy. If memory cannot be freed (the default policy is noeviction, or no key qualifies), commands marked deny-on-memory-limit get an OOM error while read-only commands such as GET keep working. Replica output buffers are outside what the limit protects: with replicas attached it is suggested to set a lower maxmemory to leave free RAM for them (not needed under noeviction), and a forked child adds copy-on-write memory pressure. The compiled default is 0 (commented out in the shipped file), and a 32-bit instance with no limit is given a 3 GB maxmemory with noeviction at startup. Whether any kind of instance ignores the limit is not stated.
answers.C: When memory use reaches maxmemory, keys are evicted according to maxmemory-policy; processCommand runs eviction before executing a command. Under the default policy, noeviction, writes return errors, and in general when no key can be evicted, write commands that need memory get errors. Which memory or which instances are exempt from the limit is not stated.
answers.D: Before running a command the server checks memory against maxmemory and, if over, tries to evict keys according to maxmemory-policy for a bounded time, continuing in a timer if needed. Writes start failing with an out-of-memory error when the policy is noeviction (the default) or when no suitable key can be evicted (for example a volatile policy with no keys that have an expire); this applies to commands that may increase memory use (SET, LPUSH, INCR, EXEC containing such commands), while read-only commands keep working. Replica output buffers (replication buffer beyond the backlog size) and the AOF buffer are subtracted from the used-memory count so that DELs generated by eviction cannot cause an eviction loop, so real memory use can exceed the limit. Replicas ignore maxmemory by default (replica-ignore-maxmemory yes) and rely on the master's DELs, so they may use more memory than the setting.

question: How does the server behave when persistence goes wrong: when a background snapshot fails, when the append-only file is damaged at startup, and when the data file cannot be loaded at all?
model_answer: If snapshots are enabled and the latest background save failed, the server by default stops accepting write commands (so the operator notices), and accepts them again once a background save succeeds; AOF write or fsync errors likewise cause writes to be denied. At startup, an AOF that is merely truncated at the end is by default loaded as far as possible with a log message, but if that option is off the server refuses to start, and an AOF corrupted in the middle always makes the server exit with an error (unless a small corrupt tail is explicitly allowed to be cut off). A fatal error loading the RDB file, or a failed AOF load, makes the server exit rather than start with partial data.
required_facts: After a failed background save (with save points configured) writes are refused by default until a save succeeds; AOF write/fsync errors also block writes
A truncated AOF tail is loaded as much as possible by default; with that option disabled the server refuses to start
Corruption in the middle of the AOF, or a fatal RDB load error, makes the server exit at startup

answers.A: The command gate includes a disk-error write refusal, so writes can be refused when there is a disk error. What specifically happens when a background snapshot fails, when the append-only file is damaged at startup, or when the data file cannot be loaded: not stated.
answers.B: After a failed background save, stop-writes-on-bgsave-error makes the server refuse writes, so the user learns the hard way that data is not persisting; the command gate checks this through writeCommandsDeniedByDiskError and returns a disk error message. With appendfsync always, a failed AOF write makes the process exit. When a preload-file backup manifest is configured, startup aborts if the target is missing or cannot be loaded. What happens when the append-only file is damaged at startup, or when the normal data file cannot be loaded, is not stated.
answers.C: If a background save fails, the server by default stops accepting writes so that the failure is noticed; processCommand refuses writes after a persistence error. Behaviour when the append only file is damaged at startup and when the data file cannot be loaded at all is not stated.
answers.D: If snapshots are enabled (at least one save point) and the latest background save failed, the server by default refuses write commands (stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes) until a background save succeeds again; AOF write or fsync errors likewise cause writes to be refused. At startup, an AOF truncated at the end is loaded as far as possible with a log message when aof-load-truncated is yes (the default), otherwise the server aborts and the file must be repaired with redis-check-aof. An AOF corrupted in the middle makes the server exit with an error; corruption at the tail can be truncated automatically only if aof-load-corrupt-tail-max-size is set above its default of 0 and the damaged part is within that size. If the AOF files cannot be opened or loaded, or the RDB file exists but fails to load, the server logs a fatal error and exits; a missing RDB file simply starts with an empty dataset.

question: What consistency and durability guarantees does master-replica replication NOT give, what can an operator configure to narrow the exposure, and how does a replica behave towards clients when its link to the master is down?
model_answer: Replication is asynchronous, so a write acknowledged by the master may not have reached any replica and can be lost on failover. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes unless at least N replicas are connected with a lag of at most M seconds, but this explicitly does not guarantee that N replicas received a given write; it only bounds the window of exposure. A replica that has lost its master, or is still synchronising, by default keeps answering queries with possibly stale or even empty data; it can instead be configured to return an error for data commands. Replicas are read-only by default, and loading a sync payload directly from the socket without first storing it on disk carries its own data-loss risks if the transfer fails.
required_facts: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost
A minimum-replicas / maximum-lag setting can make the master refuse writes, but it does not guarantee the write reached that many replicas, it only limits the exposure window
A disconnected or syncing replica serves stale (possibly empty) data by default, or can be set to reply with an error instead

answers.A: Which consistency and durability guarantees replication does not give: not stated. A min-replicas write refusal exists in the command gate, so an operator can have writes refused under a min-replicas condition; its exact semantics are not stated. The command gate also has read-only replica and stale replica checks, so a replica can refuse commands on those grounds; the precise behaviour toward clients when the master link is down: not stated.
answers.B: Replication is asynchronous, so replicas lag and acknowledged writes can be lost. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes when it does not appear connected to at least a given number of replicas (min-replicas-to-write); this does not guarantee that N replicas accept a write, it only limits the window of exposure for lost writes to the specified number of seconds. Diskless loading on a replica may cause data loss during failovers because the RDB is not immediately stored on disk, and parsing the RDB from the socket safely needs more memory. A read-only replica rejects writes from normal clients. How a replica treats clients while its link to the master is down is not stated.
answers.C: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes if it appears not to be connected to at least a given number of replicas; this does not guarantee that N replicas will accept a write, it only limits the window of exposure for lost writes to the specified number of seconds. How a replica behaves towards clients while its link to the master is down is not stated.
answers.D: Replication is asynchronous, so a write acknowledged by the master is not guaranteed to have reached any replica and can be lost on failover; replicas may serve out-of-date data. An operator can set min-replicas-to-write with min-replicas-max-lag so the master stops accepting writes when fewer than N online replicas have lag within M seconds; this does not guarantee that N replicas accepted a write, it only limits the window of exposure for lost writes to that many seconds. A larger replication backlog lets replicas resynchronise partially after longer disconnects. When a replica's link to the master is down (or sync is still in progress), with replica-serve-stale-data yes (default) it keeps answering, possibly with stale or empty data; with no it replies with a MASTERDOWN error to data commands, still allowing a small set such as INFO, REPLICAOF, AUTH, SHUTDOWN, CONFIG and pub/sub commands. Replicas are read-only by default.

question: What restrictions does running in cluster mode impose on commands and databases compared with a standalone server, and what happens to the cluster's availability when some hash slots have no serving node?
model_answer: In cluster mode a command may only address a single key or several keys that all hash to the same slot, and multi-key commands are additionally refused while that slot is being migrated; commands whose keys span slots fail with a cross-slot error, which follows from the project's position that multi-key operations cannot be distributed transparently. Only one database is available: the number of databases is forced to 1 and selecting another database is not allowed. By default, if any hash slot is uncovered the whole cluster stops accepting queries until all slots are covered again; this can be relaxed so the covered part keeps serving, and another option allows reads while the cluster is down.
required_facts: Multi-key commands must have all keys in the same hash slot, otherwise they are rejected (and are refused while the slot is unstable/migrating)
Cluster mode has a single database: the database count is forced to 1 and SELECT is not allowed
By default the cluster stops accepting queries if any slot is uncovered; an option lets the covered subset keep serving

answers.A: In cluster mode the keyspace uses one dict per hash slot (16,384), commands pass a cluster redirection check, and scripts calling into the server have cluster checks applied. What restrictions cluster mode places on commands and databases compared with standalone: not stated. What happens to availability when some hash slots have no serving node: not stated.
answers.B: A node must be started with cluster-enabled yes, since a normal instance cannot join a cluster. A request whose keys fall in different hash slots is rejected with -CROSSSLOT, and a multi-key request during a slot migration can get -TRYAGAIN; commands for slots served elsewhere are redirected with MOVED or ASK. If some hash slots are no longer covered, the whole cluster eventually becomes unavailable, a behaviour the cluster-require-full-coverage option changes. Any restriction on databases in cluster mode is not stated.
answers.C: In cluster mode multi-key operations work only when all keys are in the same hash slot, and clients whose keys live on another node are redirected. The cluster bus has no authentication of its own unless TLS is enabled for it. Restrictions on databases and what happens to availability when some slots have no serving node are not stated.
answers.D: In cluster mode there is only database 0: the database count is forced to 1, and SELECT, MOVE, SWAPDB and copying to another database are rejected. A command (or transaction) may only touch keys that all hash to the same slot; otherwise it gets a cross-slot error, and multi-key commands on a slot being migrated can get TRYAGAIN. The replicaof directive is not allowed, and commands for slots owned elsewhere are redirected instead of served. By default, if any hash slot has no serving node the whole cluster eventually stops accepting queries until all slots are covered again; cluster-require-full-coverage no lets the covered part keep serving, and cluster-allow-reads-when-down yes lets nodes serve reads for slots they believe they own while the cluster is down.
